title: Bullock explains the fifth increase and the case for waiting
summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia lifted the cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth increase of the year. At the press conference Governor Michele Bullock said the Board had revised its assessment of the Australian economy before the oil shock: domestic demand had already exceeded what the economy could supply by more than staff had thought. Higher fuel prices subsequently reduced real purchasing power and raised costs across industries. A rate rise could influence how far those costs reached other prices and what firms and households expected future inflation to be. It could do little to change the price of oil or unwind the inflation already in prospect over the next few quarters (opening statement and exchange with Patrick Commins).

Weak productivity had limited the scope to meet demand without raising prices. Investment had also surprised to the upside, particularly spending on data centres. Bullock estimated, with uncertainty, that perhaps 70% of data-centre investment was imported. The domestic share still drew builders and electricians into projects competing for scarce labour. Spending creates demand during construction; productivity gains depend on how the assets are used afterwards. Bullock saw a further reason why such gains need not lead to low rates: a rise in global demand for investment relative to saving could raise the neutral rate. She supplied no date for an AI productivity payoff. The staff’s medium-term assumptions still implied potential growth around 2% (exchanges with Jacob Shteyman, Brandon How and John Kehoe).

The six members favouring a rise gave more weight to persistent inflation. In the Governor’s account, long-term expectations still appeared anchored. Business surveys and contacts nevertheless suggested some firms were starting to regard inflation around 3.5% as normal. That figure represented conversations, rather than a measurement of the population’s expectations. Firms facing stronger costs could pass them to customers more readily while demand remained high. Households could seek wage increases to recover purchasing power. Bullock saw evidence of these pressures and expected tighter policy to weaken demand; she declined to diagnose a wage-price spiral. The three members favouring a hold put more weight on falling house prices, unemployment edging higher and the absence of an acceleration in wage growth. They wanted time to observe earlier increases (exchanges with Matthew Cranston, Stella Qiu, Sophia Rodrigues and Adrian Rollins).

Timing explains how the Board could see an extended period of above-target inflation and still leave its next move open. Bullock put the full transmission lag at roughly a year, possibly longer. Lower housing turnover cuts purchases associated with moving home. Exchange-rate changes affect prices of imported finished goods and production inputs, with pass-through taking perhaps nine to twelve months. Housing tax changes also complicated the attribution of weaker investor borrowing to interest rates alone. If housing and spending weakened much faster, unemployment could rise more sharply than in the baseline. Bullock said the downside scenario delivered relatively little extra disinflation over the coming quarters. Previous financial-stability modelling suggested arrears and negative equity could rise without threatening banks’ stability, although individual households could face severe difficulty (exchanges with Ian Verrender, Chris Kohler and Youssef Saudie).

A reporter described markets as reading the removal of earlier tightening language as dovish. Bullock explained that some of the earlier risks had moved into the central forecast. Activity risks looked more balanced and some upside inflation risk remained. The forecast assumed a cash-rate path with roughly one further increase, and neither that assumption nor the changed wording settled what the Board would do. She described the purpose of subsequent speeches as explaining how evidence informs decisions. The transcript supplies no dated market prices or measured surprise (exchanges with Cecile Lefort and Nadine Blayney).

questions.question: How much disinflation from past hikes is still in the pipeline?
questions.detail: Bullock describes falling housing turnover, softer labour demand and a lag of roughly a year. She cannot allocate the fall in investor borrowing between rates and tax changes. To judge the need for another hike, compare owner-occupier and investor lending, turnover, mortgage payments and spending on goods associated with moving. Official housing-finance data and bank portfolio disclosures could show which borrowers have already adjusted and where transmission is still to come.

questions.question: Are businesses changing their pricing rules or simply resetting prices after an input shock?
questions.detail: The Governor cites survey and liaison evidence and acknowledges that long-run expectations appear anchored. She offers no estimate of how many firms now plan repeated increases around 3.5%. Look for successive observations of selling-price intentions, wage agreements and realised services inflation across industries with different fuel exposure. RBA liaison summaries, business surveys and official price statistics would help assess the risk of persistence relevant to the front end of the curve.

questions.question: How much additional domestic capacity does the investment boom actually create?
questions.detail: Imported hardware limits the domestic construction impulse, while competition for particular trades can still make that impulse inflationary. For the medium-term rate outlook, examine the share of local work, completion dates and actual output after commissioning at data-centre projects. Construction statistics, company capital expenditure disclosures and industry productivity releases could separate pressure on scarce labour today from durable additions to the economy’s capacity.

limitation: The official transcript marks one brief follow-up from Patrick Commins as inaudible. The Governor’s preceding answer on the oil-price counterfactual is available in full.
